items: The next evening the hall of Miletus was full, for word of the song had gone through the city. And the singer took up the thread where he had cut it.
Last night you promised us a wedding on a holy mountain, father — and a golden apple. Sing it!
Patience, child. Before the apple can be thrown, the prize it buys must be born. Tonight I sing of a swan on a river — and of the most beautiful woman the sun has ever seen.
Muse, goddess of memory, sing through me again —
— sing of Sparta by the Eurotas, of the daughters of its king, and of the oath that will one day drag every king of Greece to a single war.
Hear then, as the Muse gives it: how Helen was born, and how the kings of Greece were bound.
In those days Sparta was ruled by Tyndareus — a just king grown grey in peace — and by his queen, Leda.
Their house was ordered and their land at peace. But the eye of heaven had fallen on that house.
For Zeus himself had looked on Leda — and where the king of the gods looks, fate follows.
One evening, at the hour of offerings, the queen was alone at the river.
Out of the sky came a great swan, fleeing an eagle — so it seemed.
It took shelter in the arms of the queen. And the singer will say plainly what the wise already know: the swan was Zeus, king of the gods, in a borrowed shape. The eagle too was his device.
In the fullness of time the queen was delivered — not of a child, but of a wonder: a great egg, glowing like the moon behind cloud.
This is the god's doing. What comes of it we will raise as our own — and be silent, and be glad.
And the king spoke wisely. For no house refuses what heaven sends — twice.
From the egg came four children: two daughters and two sons.
Helen and Clytemnestra; Castor and Polydeuces. Two, the wise said, were the god's children — Helen and Polydeuces. Two were the king's — Clytemnestra and Castor. All four were raised as one blood.
The boys grew into the first horsemen and boxers of Greece. Men called them the Dioscuri — the youths of Zeus.
*DIOSCURI — "the youths of Zeus," the name all Greece gave the twin brothers.

Four children of one wondrous birth. But on one of them the light fell differently. Word of the girl Helen's beauty ran through Greece like fire through summer grass — and beauty of that measure is not a gift only. It is a burden laid on the world.
Tales of the girl's beauty reached Athens, and its king — Theseus, the old slayer of the Minotaur*, greatest hero of the age before this one. Great men do not always age into wisdom.
*MINOTAUR — a bull-headed monster of Crete that Theseus slew in his youth. That tale belongs to another song.
The daughters of the gods are not too high for the son of Aegeus. We sail for Sparta.
So two aging heroes sailed to do a young men's folly — and worse than folly. What they planned was a crime against a king's house and a child's peace.
At the festival of Artemis by the river, the girls of Sparta danced.
*ARTEMIS — virgin goddess of the wild and of young girls, sister of Apollo.
And armed strangers broke the ring, and carried the child Helen away to their ship.
Against the house of a king. Against the peace of a festival. Against a child. Heaven keeps a ledger of such deeds.
Theseus hid the child at Aphidna in Attica, in the keeping of his aged mother, Aethra — meaning to wed Helen when she came of age. He himself went off after other follies. He never returned in time.
Eat, child. Your brothers will come. I know sons — and I know brothers.
The Dioscuri led the men of Sparta into Attica. Athens itself shut its gates and gave up the secret: Aphidna.
Aphidna fell in a day. The brothers took no revenge on the land — they had come for one thing only.

And they brought their sister home. One prize they took: Aethra, mother of Theseus, made handmaid to the child she had guarded. Mark that old woman well, princes. Her road runs further than any in this hall would guess — it ends on the walls of Troy.
And Theseus, father? Did he pay for it?
He paid. He came home to find Athens weary of him; he died on a small island, a king without a city. The gods are not mocked — they are only patient.
Now the years turn. The child becomes a woman — and every king in Greece turns his face toward Sparta.
Helen grew into the most beautiful woman of the age — of any age. Her sister Clytemnestra grew tall and proud beside her.
And when she came of age to marry, the heralds began to arrive. Then the kings themselves.
Every throne in Greece sends its master to my door. How does a man choose one king... and make enemies of all the rest?
They came from every kingdom: the young lords of all Greece, each with gifts to empty a treasury.

Ajax of Salamis, son of that same Telamon who was first through the wall of Troy. Diomedes of Argos. Idomeneus of Crete. And Philoctetes — bearing the great bow of Heracles himself, given to him at the hero's death. The sons of the last song stood in the court of this one.
And one wooed by proxy: for rich Mycenae, Agamemnon son of Atreus sent gifts beyond all others — on behalf of his younger brother, Menelaus.
Forty kings under one roof, wooing one woman. The wine went round, and under the laughter the hall smelled of drawn bronze.
If I choose the strongest, the rest unite against him. If I choose the richest, the proud ones burn my roof. Whichever man I name, I name a war.
Then find a man clever enough to make the choosing safe, my king. If such a man lives.
Among the last came a young king from a poor rocky island in the west: Odysseus of Ithaca. He brought no gifts. He came to watch.
For Odysseus had the gift the gods give more rarely than strength or beauty: mētis* — the cunning mind. He saw at one glance what Tyndareus feared. And he saw something else.
*MĒTIS — cunning intelligence; among the Greeks an excellence of the first rank, the special gift of the goddess Athena.

Penelope, daughter of the king's brother Icarius. Not the most beautiful woman in that palace — but the one whose eyes were quiet and deep. Odysseus made his choice in that moment, and it was not Helen.
You cannot choose a husband, king. But I can make the choosing safe — so safe that no sword leaves its sheath, now or after.
Untie this knot, Ithacan, and name your price.
My price is a marriage — but not Helen's. Speak for me to your brother Icarius. I ask for Penelope.

This was Odysseus's device. Before any man was chosen, EVERY suitor swore the great oath upon the sacrifice: to defend the marriage of Helen's husband — WHOEVER he might be — against any man on earth who should ever take her from him.

So every rival became a guardian, and the choosing was made safe. But hear it, princes: an oath is a seed. This one lay quiet in the ground for years — and when it broke the earth at last, it dragged every king who swore it, and their ships and their sons, across the sea to Troy.
Then the king chose — and the tradition is honest about the reasons: he chose the wealth and power of Mycenae.
Menelaus, younger son of Atreus, backed by his brother Agamemnon's gifts. The sons of the cursed house of Mycenae had risen high indeed.
And no sword left its sheath. The oath held them all — as it would hold them all again.
The wedding of Helen and Menelaus was the greatest festival Sparta had ever seen. The singers sang till dawn.
And Tyndareus, grown old, gave more than his daughter: in time the rule of Sparta itself would pass to Helen's husband.
So Helen was wed, and Sparta rejoiced. Whether Helen rejoiced, the songs do not say. Remember that too.
Then Tyndareus paid Odysseus's price. He spoke to his brother Icarius — and Icarius could not refuse the man who had saved the peace of Greece. But his heart refused.
So Odysseus wed Penelope — a small wedding after the great one, and the happier of the two.
Stay in Sparta, both of you! I will build you a house by my own — daughter, do not go to that rock in the sea!
And when they set out for Ithaca, Icarius followed the chariot on foot, begging his daughter to stay.
I will not steal a wife. Choose freely, lady: your father's house — or my road.

Penelope said no word. She drew her veil over her face — and that was her whole answer. Her father let her go, and on that spot he raised a shrine to Aidōs* — to Modesty herself. Mark this woman, princes. Twenty years from now, all the manhood of an island will break against her quiet will.
*AIDŌS — reverent modesty and shame before the eyes of others; among the Greeks, a virtue with the force of law.
Ithaca is a poor island — rock, goats, and good harbors. Odysseus would not have traded it for Mycenae.

With his own hands he built their marriage bed — and he built it around a living olive tree rooted in the earth, so that the bed could never be moved without killing the tree. Only two living souls would ever know that secret. Remember the olive-tree bed, princes. At the far end of this whole long song, everything will turn upon it.
And there, for a while, the story leaves them: a clever king, a quiet queen, a poor island, and a happiness the great palaces might have envied.
And the elder sister? Agamemnon of Mycenae, not content with making his brother a king, took Clytemnestra for himself. The two thrones of the Peloponnese now shared one blood twice over.
The feast was magnificent. But this was the hall of Atreus — the hall of the terrible supper of the last song. Old blood does not wash out of stones.

And far away, in exile, the boy from the last song — Aegisthus, son of Thyestes — had grown to manhood, nursing one lesson: remember Mycenae. Remember the feast. The threads are laid, princes. The loom only waits.
So the two sisters of the egg were parted to the two greatest thrones of Greece.
Helen, queen of Sparta. Clytemnestra, queen of Mycenae.
They loved each other, after the way of sisters. And each, in the end, will be the ruin of her own house — one by leaving it, and one by staying. But that is far ahead of us.
One more thing happened at Helen's wedding, and the singer keeps it for last.
Over the feast an eagle stooped and took a white dove, in the sight of all.
Zeus of the omens... what have you written over this marriage?
The guests laughed and drank. Two men in that court did not laugh. Remember which two.
And above the clouds, the plan of Zeus moved forward — the plan made with Themis in the first song, to ease the Earth of her burden by a great war.

The beauty is born, and wed where you appointed. The kings of Greece are bound by their own oath — one rope through every royal hall. And Troy in the east grows rich, and its old debt to Apollo and Poseidon stands unpaid.
Then all the pieces stand upon the board. Let the mortals move them now — each by his own choice. That is how my plan always walks: on the feet of men's own wills.
And Troy? Troy had rebuilt, and grown richer than ever under the boy-king of the last song — Priam the purchased, now grown grey and great, father of fifty sons.
He still wore the small gold pendant of his boyhood — the ransomed boy who had watched his city burn, now the richest king of the east.
And in his wall, rebuilt by the hands of men, the fated stretch stood where it had always stood. The gods' wage was still owed. The gods were still patient.
Then the war was already certain, father — before Helen ever left her husband's hall? Before any wrong was done?
Certain as harvest after sowing, child. The field was sown: the beauty, the oath, the unpaid debt in the east.

And yet — mark it well — every man and woman in this song will walk to that war on their own feet, by their own choices. The gods set the board. They do not move the hands. Both things are true at once. That is the oldest riddle in the song, and I will not solve it for you. No singer can.
Enough for one night. The bride is born and wed. The kings are bound. The east is rich and owing.
And tomorrow, father? The mountain? The apple?

Tomorrow, if the Muse is willing: a wedding of a goddess to a mortal man, with every god among the guests — one goddess uninvited at the door — a golden apple thrown among three queens of heaven... and far away on a mountain called Ida, a herdsman who does not know he is a prince of Troy.
"The gods weave ruin into the lives of men, so that there may be song for the generations to come."
— after words spoken in the song of the return, in the hall of a sea-king.
